text:
Genesis 22 yields most to one who observes its omissions. Sarah has no place in the chapter, and in the next verse the book announces her death. Nothing is said which directly connects that death with the mountain; yet the scene leaves the household altered, as if something had not come back from the trial. Abraham returns to the servants; Isaac is not named in the return. At the very point where a meaner story would have dwelt upon embrace, explanation, or recovery, the narration withdraws. The silence is more than a blank in the record; it has the force of testimony.

It may be answered that this is only the ordinary economy of ancient narrative, which rarely reports feeling and never explains. This may perhaps, in some sense, be true. Yet the narrator elsewhere gives the inward sign plainly enough: Esau cries out; Jacob is afraid; Joseph weeps. The reserve here, therefore, is chosen. There is knowledge in the handling. Restraint, in this voice, becomes accusation.
